The incubation period of the Common diving petrel (Pelecanoides urinatrix) concludes with hatching after approximately 46 days [ab = approximately 46 days] at a stable nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that aligns closely with the 44-to-52-day range reported in the literature for this species. The newly emerged chick, termed a downy nestling, weighs roughly 17 grams [Wwb = roughly 17 grams] at the moment of hatching, reflecting the modest initial mass typical of petrel chicks that must then undergo a prolonged period of rapid mass gain fueled by parental provisioning of lipid-rich stomach oil. This neonatal body mass is derived from an egg weight that can range from 15.5 to 21.5 grams, with a reported mean of 18.84 grams, so the hatchling represents the lower end of that potential spectrum. The chick remains entirely dependent on its parents for thermoregulation and nourishment during the first few days post-hatch, a period characterized by brooding and frequent small meals.

After hatching, the nestling enters a phase of accelerated somatic growth within the burrow, culminating in the achievement of first flight. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of active metabolic periods in this species, approximately 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], fledging occurs at roughly 50 days after hatching [tx = roughly 50 days after hatching]. This developmental milestone, marking the transition from a sedentary, brooded chick to a fledgling capable of sustained flight, is preceded by the attainment of an asymptotic mass of 160 grams [Wwi = 160 grams] just prior to nest departure. Interestingly, this ultimate pre-fledging weight exceeds the mean adult body mass of 128.6 grams, as documented by Paynter and Prin in 1979, suggesting that chicks accumulate substantial fat reserves to buffer the energetic challenges of the post-fledging period. The fledgling must then rapidly refine its foraging skills to achieve nutritional independence, a critical juncture in the species' life history.

Sexual maturation in the Common diving petrel is a relatively protracted process for a bird of its size, constrained by the need to attain full physiological competence for breeding. In the same thermal environment characteristic of the species' active metabolism (39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]), puberty is estimated to be reached at around 150 days after hatching [tp = around 150 days after hatching]. This tempo of gonadal development appears somewhat slower than that of many other small seabirds, potentially reflecting the energetic demands of their specialized diving foraging strategy. The post-fledging juvenile and subadult periods are thus of considerable duration, with young birds gradually acquiring the flight muscle strength and diving proficiency necessary for successful prey capture in the cold, productive waters of the Southern Ocean. During this pre-reproductive interval, immature individuals continue to grow and refine their hunting techniques.

First reproduction in the wild is a deferred event, with individuals typically initiating their first breeding attempt at an age of about 2 years since birth [tR = about 2 years since birth], subject to the same core body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This two-year delay to first brood, with some sources suggesting an onset as late as three years, is common among Procellariiformes and reflects the considerable investment required to secure a burrow, form a pair bond, and successfully incubate a single-egg clutch. The species' maximum reproductive rate is quite low, with females laying just a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and typically only one clutch annually [F_R_i = one clutch annually], a strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity in a resource-variable environment. This low fecundity is offset by high adult survival rates, a classic demographic trade-off among long-lived pelagic seabirds that face unpredictable food availability.

Longevity data for the Common diving petrel indicate a maximum lifespan in the wild of approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years], considerably longer than the 6.5-year benchmark reported in the Encyclopedia of Life, though consistent with the extended lifespans documented across the Procellariiformes at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This relatively long lifespan for a small seabird is matched by the species' consistent annual breeding output. Life history theory predicts that such a combination of low fecundity, delayed maturity, and a moderately extended adult phase is adaptive in a stable but unpredictable pelagic environment where adult survival is paramount. The species' burrow-nesting habit and reliance on krill and small fish further shape its demographic schedule, with the entire life cycle finely tuned to the cyclical productivity of the Southern Ocean ecosystem.
